name: Palmitoyl hexapeptide-12
evidenceNote: The published work is cell studies, lab tests on donated skin, and safety patch tests. No independent placebo-controlled trial of this peptide on its own in people has been published.
summary: Palmitoyl hexapeptide-12 is a fatty-acid-linked elastin fragment used in anti-aging skincare. It is a cosmetic ingredient, not an FDA-approved drug.
keyTakeaway: Palmitoyl hexapeptide-12 is the six-amino-acid sequence VGVAPG, a repeating unit of the skin protein elastin, with a palmitic acid tail added so it sinks into the outer skin. It appears in anti-aging creams and serums at very low concentrations, reported up to 20 parts per million. Lab work shows the bare fragment draws skin fibroblasts toward it, and a 2025 study on donated human skin found the peptide forms a gel that stiffened a damaged skin barrier. Proof that it smooths wrinkles in people is thin. It is regulated as a cosmetic, which needs no FDA approval, and a US industry safety panel judged it safe as used.

blocks.text: Palmitoyl hexapeptide-12 is a skincare ingredient made of six amino acids, valine, glycine, valine, alanine, proline and glycine (written VGVAPG), joined to palmitic acid, a common fatty acid [2]. The VGVAPG sequence repeats many times in elastin, the stretchy protein that lets skin spring back after it is pinched [4].

The fatty tail is there to help a water-loving peptide get into the oily outer layer of skin. In lab measurements, adding the palmitoyl tail to an elastin-like peptide made it stick to skin proteins about ten times more than the same peptide without it, possibly because the molecules clump into self-assembled aggregates [3]. A related ingredient, myristoyl hexapeptide-12, uses a different fatty acid on the same sequence [2].

In ingredient lists it is named on its own or appears inside blends, sometimes listed as palmitoyl oligopeptide. Cosmetic chemists group it with matrikines, short peptides copied from pieces of the skin's support structure that are thought to signal repair [2].

The original idea comes from a 1984 study showing that VGVAPG on its own attracts fibroblasts, the cells that build collagen and elastin, and monocytes, a type of immune cell. The effect was strongest at very low concentrations and could be blocked by an antibody against elastin, suggesting the cells recognize it as a piece of elastin [4]. The theory behind the cosmetic use is that a fragment like this tells skin cells that elastin has been broken down and needs rebuilding.

A second possible action is physical. A 2025 study applied a 1 percent solution of the peptide to full-thickness human skin donated after surgery and tracked it with mass spectrometry imaging. The peptide passed through the outer stratum corneum into the epidermis, where it picked up calcium and other ions already in the skin and set into a gel. After the skin's own fats were stripped away, treated samples recovered stiffness and barrier properties in mechanical testing [1].

A 2026 safety framework ran the sequence through six bioinformatic tools. They matched it to the chemotactic region of human elastin and flagged no toxin or allergen signals [2]. These are lab and computer findings; none measure wrinkles on a living face.

No, and as a cosmetic ingredient it does not need to be. Under US law, cosmetics and their ingredients, apart from color additives, do not require FDA approval before sale. Whether a product counts as a cosmetic or a drug depends on its intended use, so a cream that claims to change the structure or function of the skin, rather than its appearance, can be treated as a drug [5].

In the US, ingredient safety is reviewed by an expert body called the Cosmetic Ingredient Review (CIR). Its 2018 assessment of hexapeptide-12 and its fatty acid versions found palmitoyl hexapeptide-12 safe in cosmetics at the uses and concentrations then reported [2]. The data it relied on included a human repeat insult patch test in 53 adults that found no irritation or allergy, and leave-on products reported concentrations up to 20 ppm [2].

The strongest published evidence concerns how the peptide behaves, not whether it changes how skin looks. The donated-skin study shows it penetrates the upper layers and forms a gel, and the 1984 cell study shows the bare fragment draws fibroblasts in a dish [1][4]. Reviews cite topical testing in which the peptide improved elasticity and tone, but those results have not been confirmed in an independent, placebo-controlled trial of palmitoyl hexapeptide-12 used alone [1].

blocks.text: Most commercial skincare combines several peptides with moisturizers, retinoids or sunscreen, which makes it hard to credit any single ingredient with a visible result. There is also an open scientific question worth knowing about. Researchers studying aging have proposed that elastin fragments released naturally from arteries, lungs and skin enter the bloodstream and feed low-grade inflammation [6]. That work concerns fragments the body makes itself; the CIR data indicate very little cosmetic peptide passes through the skin [2].
